summary: The note describes the fictional Deepfake Diplomacy Crisis, which began on September 15, 2023, when a forged video showed French President Amelie Durand discussing a NATO withdrawal with a Russian intelligence chief. It covers the responses of world leaders, further deepfakes targeting other leaders, a detection technology arms race, economic fallout, and platform and regulatory responses, including the proposed Geneva Protocol on Digital Authenticity.
one_line: A deepfake video of France's president sparked a global diplomatic crisis, prompting summits, detection tech races, market turmoil, and a proposed Geneva Protocol on Digital Authenticity.
key_facts: On September 15, 2023, a deepfake video showed French President Amelie Durand in a purportedly secret conversation with Russian Intelligence Chief Igor Petrokov about France withdrawing from NATO.
Cyber-security firms and intelligence agencies revealed within hours that the Durand video was synthetic.
The G20 Summit was hastily convened in Brussels on October 3, 2023, to address the crisis.
Japanese Prime Minister Hiroshi Tanaka called for an International Task Force on Digital Integrity, calling deepfakes an 'existential threat' to trust in diplomacy.
Amelie Durand addressed the European Parliament on October 8, calling the deepfake 'an act of digital warfare'.
On November 1, new deepfakes targeted Canadian Prime Minister Michael Bennett (a faked tirade against immigrants) and Brazilian President Carlos Mendez (negotiating bribes with a drug cartel).
UN Secretary-General Ana-Maria Lopez convened an emergency meeting, saying 'The digital realm is now a theater of conflict.'
By December 2023, CyberGuard Technologies unveiled an AI algorithm that detects deepfake videos with 98.7% accuracy; Dr. Emily Huang is its leading researcher.
On December 20, the Dow Jones fell 800 points after a falsified video of the U.S. Treasury Secretary announcing trade policy changes with China; it was debunked within hours.
The International Chamber of Commerce issued guidelines for validating digital content.

On January 10, 2024, Nexa, GlobalBook, and Bwitter testified before the European Union's Commission on Digital Safety; Nexa CEO Alexander Mendoza spoke on protecting reality without compromising free speech.
A symposium in Geneva on February 15, 2024, drafted the proposed 'Geneva Protocol on Digital Authenticity' to frame ethical use of synthetic media and punish malicious deployment.
